text: The Human Machine Interaction has a big role in the user approach with households appliances. During the main phase (the use one), users are called to manage energy choices, often without available efficient information regarding the best behavior they can adopt. At the end, people usually don't pay the attention that a sustainable behavior is supposed to need, wasting consequently energy, this both because of a bad education and an uncompleted communication around the appliance. The product informs users through its physical data and its "collateral communication" (manuals, brochures, websites...). With this paper I will analyze how appliances reach -and don't reach-the final user to suggest him or her the best behavior to save energy. A correct information approach helps a correct appliance use, influencing users' choices and implementing their sustainable knowledge. After a deep analysis of the state of the art, this paper will suggest different interaction ways, to guide people behavior in the households appliances usage, to reach the goal of a sustainable approach. Is it possible to increase energy saving in the appliances use phase? Should the product itself be reviewed, or just its collateral communication, or both? Which are the worst interaction elements able to confuse the user? Which are the best ones? How could designers project appliances in order to create best products and best behaviors? Can some cross interaction solution help user/appliances relationship? And which role should technology have in this challenge?

text: INTRODUCTION
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: The highest energy waste in the domestic area depends, after heating, on households appliances (25% ca.), as several studies declare. The problem is strictly connected to the use phase, and companies well know the argument.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Approximately 90% of the total environmental impact during the life of a product from the white goods industry occurs during the utilization of the product. The impact [...] is in part determined by the performance of the product, which is specified during the design and product development phase. But most of the impact during this phase is determined by how the consumer actually uses the appliance, since our products are to a very high degree interactive. Once the product is brought, the best way to use it and useful suggestions for a better sustainable behavior are not clearly communicated. Often users (especially European ones) invest more money to buy a high efficient appliance, but they don't suppose a better usage conduct to a lower power consumption. So, it's possible -and common-that a rough interaction limits appliances energy saving. The issue is that the appliance is designed for thousand people. One product, thousand people. But users are different: different ages, sex, educational levels, economic availabilities and mental schemes. And this produces different interactions, of course. Partner in this crime is that communication around the product is not satisfactory: user manuals don't deal with sustainable specific instructions, programs and interfaces aren't clear, advertising often speaks about sustainability without giving the exact idea about how to be sustainable with the product, and the only consultable suggestions are generic, regarding appliance typology and not referring to the specific model.

text: At the state of the art households appliances can communicate with user in two different ways: with the product collateral communication, that regards the product but isn't part of it (advertising, brochure, manuals...) and the communication through the product, connected with interfaces and users/appliances relationship. This one should be as simple and intuitive as possible, but generally -as we will see in a whileconnection is not immediate.

text: Collateral Communication
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Appliance collateral communication is an addendum to the "natural" product communication potential. It concretizes in brochures, booklets, leaflets that generally give general suggestions, similar to the on line findable ones. There are no particular details about the specific product, interface, model; for clear reasons. But the same is for manuals, that, for contrary, would be supposed to give e deeper detail (just thinking about the name "instruction manual"). For this research 52 manuals have been examined, regarding washingmachines, cooktops, dishwashings, ovens and fridges from companies as Electrolux, Rex, Zanussi, Bosch, Smeg, Whirlpool, Whestinghouse and Indesit. The aim was discover the general approach to user manual definition. The parameters searched into each manual were: One manual for one product; > 10pp. long; Generic sustainable suggestions; Specific sustainable suggestions; Interface explanations; Detailed usage instructions; Dismission instructions; Maintenance suggestions; Graphic care. It came out that the existing tendency is to put sustainable suggestions and info in small, not easy to find, parts of the manual. Just in rare cases manual really explains the best way to use thatspecific-appliance. Generally, when present, environmental indications deal with packaging disposal or general suggestions (it's common to have a manual for many appliances, i.e. for 4 or 5 models). But every company has its tendency. It could also happen that given instruction are so complete that a "sustainable" dedicated space in summary becomes no necessary (even if this could be positive for user consultation). In this cases sustainability is treated as one requirement and not the -or centralrequirement (as should be in the entire design process). Specific info are important to guide a correct behavior. If in a dishwasher the (eventual) difference between ECO and QUICK program is explained, this can avoid incorrect washings and consequent lacks of confidence. But from analysis appears that attention to both generic and specific suggestions is not common. In particular, Anglo-Saxons manuals demonstrate still less attention. Average lack values are: manual/product direct reference, sustainability suggestions (with some exception for specific models and specific companies). Sometimes, also interface description is not exhaustive.

Norman says: <<When technology is not designed from a human-centered point of view, it doesn't reduce the incidence of human error nor minimize the impact when errors do occur>>. This is particularly true concerning energetic products. text: Case Studies
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: To understand the real human/appliances interaction some observation have been conducted, to permit behavioral and mental schemes appliances approach analysis. A website (www.videocap.annina.ufobestianera.com), posted on social networks, widespread by mail, paper and and voice was realized to reach people asking them for videos regarding appliances usage. As often as not people felt necessary verbal explication of their actions. This permitted an important information collection, not just regarding appliance usage, but also daily interactive attitudes. Thanks to video analysis, schematized in sheets, some shared cases came out:
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: 1. The idea that the program that needs less resources (water, energy, time etc.) cannot be efficient as the ones that need more energy cost; 2. Personal mental scheme projection on appliance usage. For example, the belief that in the washing machine soap tray just liquid soap can be poured in; 3. The lack of confidence with dishwasher that makes people raise the dishes before washing them with the appliances, despite (quite) all manuals define this as a behavior to avoid. Some questionnaires, drew up in 3 times and structured with the aim to analyze deeply and one by one every white good, has been administrated both on paper and on web. Results confirmed video data and underlined the avoiding appliance sustainable usage tendency. Finally, analysis demonstrated that, based on a limited interaction (given by a poor, sometimes evasive collateral communication, and by a communication trough the product made by unclear and rigid interfaces) user is commonly confused from a sustainable (and not only) point of view. In particular, some differences came out, depending on user/machine different relationship (guys are more relaxed with technologies, elderly don't take care of environmental questions, people that want to adopt a sustainable approach generally refer to general suggestions). The main effort has human > appliance direction: the machine needs a human attitude to be understood.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: WHAT CAN IMPROVE INTERACTION?
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: People can be environmentally responsible choosing transports, shopping, dismissing waste. People can be sustainable in their home, checking their energy consumptions and choosing to limit them. During last years several monitoring devices have been invented, to help users to be as conscious as possible in their behavior. Several energy consumption communication waysmore or less efficient-can today tell people how much energy they are wasting or saving. Some interfaces are clear, others are not. The point is that one product is exactly the same for thousand people. If the majority of users can understand device communication method, we could define it a good system. Differently, a big communication problem will be present. From analysis comes out that a common language, able to explain basis sustainable characteristics is missing. Icons, symbols, colors are often different in different systems or devices (such as green and red, that, in different products, switch their meanings to indicate the same concept). This, of course, make user confused. If this is the moment to develop all this kind of devices, why don't adopt this as an opportunity to construct a common language? In particular, for interaction design it could be useful follow some roles, that, in Saffer's opinion, can guide a good design.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: [...] certainly in some circumstances, some of these characteristics may not be appropriate -you may not want a mission control panel to be playful, for example-but in general, if a product or service can be described with these adjectives, it is likely an example of good interaction design. Adjectives are: Trustworthy (because every object should inject trust in its user); Appropriate (referring to context -cultural, temporal, environmental...-); Clever (to «predict needs of [...] users and then fulfill those needs in unexpected pleasing way» [17:.66]); Ludic, (because as children we learn through play); Pleasurable (both from an aesthetical and functional points of view). But other adjectives came out as important parameters. For example, the one that Saffer defines as "clever" could be, in some cases, Automatic. Another one is Clear (if interface is clear user can correctly interpret it); or Immediate (that help to make a clear interaction); Complete (to avoid cut and partial messages to users). Different solutions were compared: Green Kitchenfoot_1 by Whirlpool, Electrolux Social appliances, mobile applications (Current State, Alert Me, Tendril, Energy UFO), travel software (ecoDrive by Fiat, eQmotion by Lampo, Ecopassenger by Trenitalia), devices for energy monitoring (Ted 5000 and Google Power Meter, Wattson by diKyoto, Holmes, EcoDhome). It came out that everything that is not clear and has a vertical communication (and that doesn't have a dialog with user) is not reactive. At the same time monologue avoids cleverness. It's to be considered that everything depends on interface and its aims. So, if the goal is data consulting, so a monologue could work. But, to explain different approaches and sensitize user behavior, a dialogue is preferable. In the analyzed cases of dialogue (i.e. for mobile application where software asks and users answers and vice versa) the context constructs a playful situation, more "educative" than monological ones. It's surely fundamental define target and capabilities to construct the perfect interaction. In other words, it's necessary define use context, moreover if energy saving has an important role. This, in fact, is the first of the guide lines for responsible interaction design.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: NEW DESIGNING BRIEF PROPOSAL
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Households appliances don't always communicate why they're working in certain way, and manuals are often curt. Technological (or "clever") product presence is positive when it doesn't give problems to user. When this is supposed to solve product problem, things became more complicated. User, as seen during observations, doesn't act in the "correct" way, but projects his/her mental schemes on the appliance, creating atypical situations, out of designers' previsions. This because one product is expected to interact with several people typologies. If design process would be based on people categories, it could be possible create appliances with intrinsic characteristics for that particular user. I'm not reffering to marketing strategies, but to design approach. Until now just a few initiatives has been taken following users' characteristics. It's possible to generate some users' groups to be taken in consideration during the designing phase, following social and demographic studies. [10] The next one would just be a possible classification hypothesis (and it's necessary to consider that households evolve). So, singles, as young couples, could be hypothetically defined as "young"; households with or without children, between 40 to 60 years old, could be hypothetically defined as "classic" and couples over 60s, as "easy". Let's take this classification into consideration for further steps.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Personalization
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Personalizing his/her appliances, user can improve object usability. It's not about cut functions, but render more immediate some (now) hidden possibilities -i.e combined ovens--. This guide line can be related also to educational topics, such as sustainability: a washing machine could suggest, depending on clothes typology, a less temperature or time level washing to save energy. Personalization can regard:
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: --interface appearance (to improve its legibility); --functions organizations (to let peopole choose commands hierarchy); --behaviors management (to register, for example, more used commands); --additional modalities activation (as suggestions).

text: Automation
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: In psychology there is a concept defined as "drop in vigilance". Norman tells that people that are not asked to have a role in the process, will lose easily their attention. Here what happens: where half automation occurs, user less attention level. This make him/her not prepared in case of inconvenience or where his/her intervention is (half) requested. At the end, if it's not possible to have a complete automation, it's necessary to well decide what should be automatized, and how.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Automation can:
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: --completely relieve users from their assignments (i.e. letting them just on/off choice); --facilitate some decisions (suggesting solutions depending on date recorded); --solve unexpected situations (i.e. automatically contacting an assistance center if necessary). Automation level, as personalization one, depends a lot on referring user. For example, easy users' category could appreciate more a complete automation than young one. The changing factor is the product and interface complexity level, that automation potentially contribute deeply to change.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Feedback
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Substantially, feedback is communication. For this reason it can regard input, when product signals user command has been understood and output, for example to communicate the end of a command, but also usage. In this case product confirms users injected process. Feedback should be quick and frequent. Every person using a product or a service should have a confirm back. Frequently, if there isn't an immediate nor clear feedback, users will do again the action they are used to do. Let's think of a person turning the oven on, before have put the food to be cooked inside. If the oven would ask confirm back or propose to turn itself on just once the dish is inside, we would have a different solution, surely more ecological. If the oven itself would suggest a low temperature, but combined with ventilated program (of course taking in consideration the food that has to be cooked) would contribute to an user's behavior improvement. The same for washing machine: once program, washing length and clothes characteristics have been chosen, system can provide a more sustainable option (i.e. less temperature water, shorter washing program). The aim would be to communicate user the possibility to have different, better, choices.
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Discretion
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: Household appliance should be as less invasive as possible. Related to sustainability, it would be precious to have a "plastic" language, suggesting (adopting money or ethic) or taking autonomous choices or commenting, depending on user' typology. In particular, discretion it's necessary to:
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: --Avoid reproaches, that cause discomfort; --Avoid repetitions, that tire and discourage people. A clear and immediate language is preferable; --Avoid irritating noises. Create new sounds for natural feedback doesn't mean irritating sound generation. All these guide lines should be adopted to create different products, depending on people they are designated. Distinguish users permit a classification and generation of products on different complexity levels. To different abilities, in fact, different difficulties can match.

text: CONCLUSIONS
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: This study, coming from my PhD thesis, wants to refer to product and interface designers to help them designing appliances as near to people as possible. After analysis, two are the emerging solutions: a complete automation or methods to educate user. Sustainable behavior depends on appliance, but also on people/machine interaction. For good interaction, appliance should be clear and immediate. It should go toward user, don't expecting the contrary. It's not about choosing "the man who do at the expense of the man who control". It's about understand which man can do, and which can just control. One appliance is designed for thousand people, who have different mental schemes. And the object, at the moment, hasn't got logical bonds to avoid misunderstandings. A clear interface is needed and designers have to design it in the best way. At the moment, confirmed by analysis, bad points in appliances communication are:
source_title: Users and households appliances: design suggestions for a better, sustainable interaction

text: --Not clear communication, collateral or around the product; --Complexity in interactive function structure; --Users' mental schemes projection on appliances functions; --Low energy saving methods knowledge;
